sections.title: The Reason for the Mitzva of Ḥalla from Bread
sections.html:
It is a mitzva to set aside from dough intended for making bread a gift of ḥalla for the kohen, and the kohen and his family members make breads and cakes from it and eat them in purity, so that they can fulfill their spiritual mission of teaching Torah to Israel. As it is stated (Bamidbar 15:17-21): "And the Lord spoke to Moshe, saying: Speak to the Children of Israel and say to them: When you come into the land to which I am bringing you, then it shall be that when you eat of the bread of the land, you shall set apart a gift to the Lord. Of the first of your dough you shall set apart a cake (ḥalla) as a gift; as the gift of the threshing floor, so shall you set it apart. Of the first of your dough you shall give to the Lord a gift throughout your generations."

Bread, which is man's principal food, expresses to a great extent the special character of man, who has the ability to choose, to create and to perfect. For all animals eat natural foods, such as grasses, leaves, grains, vegetables, fruits and even meat, whereas man eats bread, whose process of preparation is long and complex and requires the performance of many labors: plowing the soil, sowing the grain, reaping the ears, separating the grain kernels from the ears and the chaff through threshing, winnowing and sorting, grinding the kernels into flour, kneading it with water to make it into dough, and baking it. Of all the foods that man eats, the production process of bread is the most complex and sophisticated. As with bread, so with man: all the animals in the world learn, in a short time and naturally, how to survive and to be fruitful and multiply, whereas man needs to learn over many years how to obtain food, clothing and a dwelling for himself and to establish a family. And in the course of this he learns to harness the immense forces of nature to his service. The ability to choose, learn, create and perfect is the expression of the Divine image in man.

However, man may turn his powers to evil – to be haughty toward his fellows, to lie and steal, to destroy and betray – in order to increase his desires. Through the prohibition of eating bread from which ḥalla has not been separated, a person remembers God, who created all his creative powers, and takes care not to use them for evil. Through the mitzva of giving the ḥalla to the kohen, the bread and the process of its preparation become connected to holiness, and those who eat from it can elevate and direct their creative power toward goodness and blessing. This is what the Sages said (Vayikra Rabba 15:6): "Whoever fulfills the mitzva of ḥalla, it is as if he has abolished idolatry, and whoever neglects the mitzva of ḥalla, it is as if he has upheld idolatry." The broad meaning of the concept "idolatry" is all the evil deeds that a person does for the idols of his money, his lust and his pride.

The Sages further said that man himself is "the ḥalla of the world": the Holy One, blessed be He, created the earth and all the materials within it, kneaded it with the rainwater, and from the "dough" that was formed He created all the plants and animals, and from within the "dough" He separated "ḥalla," and from it He created man in His image, so that he would lead the world for the good. And when Adam sinned, he rendered himself and the whole world impure. In order to rectify his sin, Israel was commanded to separate ḥalla for the kohen and to keep it in purity, in order to remember their destiny. And this mitzva belongs more to the woman, for she has more power to direct the forces within man and thereby rectify the sin (see Bereshit Rabba 14:1; 17:7-8).

The Sages said (there 1:4): "In the merit of three things the world was created: in the merit of ḥalla, in the merit of ma'asrot, and in the merit of bikkurim." For these three mitzvot are called "reshit" (first), and they remind us that the first aim of creation is to reveal holiness within the world. Bikkurim and terumot and ma'asrot are given from the produce that grows naturally. In the merit of the bikkurim, one connects to the overall vision of the people of Israel (above 7:15), and in the merit of terumot and ma'asrot, the blessing spreads to the fields and the crops (above 7:13). The ḥalla is given from the work of a person's hands, and in its merit he merits that blessing rest upon the work of his hands and upon his home, as it is stated (Yeḥezkel 44:30): "And the first of your dough you shall give to the kohen – to cause a blessing to rest upon your house."

sections.title: The Uniqueness of Ḥalla
sections.html:
Ḥalla is one of the twenty-four gifts that Israel was commanded to give to the kohanim, so that they would be free of the burden of earning a livelihood and could fulfill their sacred mission of educating Israel in Torah, mitzvot and good character traits. Among all the gifts, the gift of "ḥalla" had special importance, for from it the kohanim prepared bread, which is man's principal food. In addition, through the mitzva of ḥalla a continuous connection was created between the Yisraelim and the kohanim. Unlike terumot and ma'asrot from fruit and grain, which the owners of the fields would distribute in the fields in large quantities several times a year, ḥalla would be given every single day, from each Israelite woman to her neighbor, the wife of a kohen, and thus all of Israel would connect to sacred values while preparing their bread.

When ḥalla is separated, the ḥalla becomes sanctified like terumah: it is forbidden for Yisraelim and Levites to eat it, and the kohanim must be careful to eat it in purity, as it is stated (Bamidbar 15:20): "as the gift of the threshing floor, so shall you set it apart." Therefore, the Yisraelim must be very careful not to render it impure, for if it becomes impure, it becomes forbidden to eat. And there was a difficulty in this, because the rule is that produce can become impure only after it has been made wet with water, in order to wash it or to prepare it as food or for another purpose; but produce that has not yet been made wet cannot become impure. Therefore, there is no problem for the Yisraelim to separate terumot from produce, since they separate them from produce that has not been made wet. But in the mitzva of ḥalla, one becomes obligated only after mixing the flour with water and making dough from it. And if the one preparing the dough is impure, he renders the dough impure with his hands and causes the ḥalla to be impure, and thereby he disgraces the mitzva and causes the loss of the ḥalla. Therefore, when the woman who kneaded the dough was impure because of her nidda or other impurities, she would call her neighbor, the wife of a kohen, to knead the dough for her, and the Israelite woman would recite the blessing over separating the ḥalla, and the kohen's wife would take her ḥalla (Yerushalmi Ḥalla 3:1). In this way the connection between the families of the Yisraelim and the families of the kohanim grew very strong.1

By Torah law ḥalla has no fixed measure, but the Sages instituted that every person should separate at least one twenty-fourth of the dough (about 4%), so that his giving would have significance. And a baker who earns his living from baking bread, since he is stingy with the gift he must give the kohen, should give at least one forty-eighth (about 2%). And since his dough is usually large, even one forty-eighth amounts to a fine gift. When the dough became impure unintentionally, even a person at home should separate the lower measure, one forty-eighth, since in any case the kohen cannot eat it (Mishna Ḥalla 1:9; 2:7; Yerushalmi 2:3; SA YD 328:1).

sections.title: The Mitzva in the Land and Outside the Land
sections.html:
The mitzva of ḥalla, like the mitzva of terumot and ma'asrot, is dependent on the Land, as it is stated (Bamidbar 15:18-19): "When you come into the land to which I am bringing you … when you eat of the bread of the land, you shall set apart a gift to the Lord." An additional condition in these mitzvot is that the majority of Israel reside in the Land, as it is stated (there 18): "When you come (be-vo'akhem) into the land" – "be-vo'akhem" means "when all of you come, and not when some of you come" (Ketubot 25a). We learn a great principle from this: the ability to reveal holiness in nature depends on the people of Israel, who were created in order to reveal the word of God, living in the Land of Israel, which was created so that holiness would be revealed through it.

However, there is a difference between the mitzvot: the mitzva of terumot and ma'asrot applies to produce that grew in the Land and whose processing was completed in the Land, even if it is taken out of the Land (above 8:9), whereas the mitzva of ḥalla depends on the kneading of the dough: if the dough was kneaded in the Land, even if the flour is from grain grown outside the Land, one must separate ḥalla from it; and if the dough was kneaded outside the Land, even if the flour is from grain of the Land of Israel, it is exempt from the mitzva of ḥalla (Yerushalmi Ḥalla 2:1). In the course of this we learn that there is special value to the creations that Israel creates in the Land of Israel, even when the materials were brought from outside the Land, and therefore they must be sanctified by setting aside ḥalla.

Following the exile of Israel in the days of the destruction of the First Temple, the majority of Israel was no longer in the Land, and the mitzva lapsed. Even in the days of the building of the Second Temple, the mitzva did not return to its place, since the majority of Israel remained in exile. However, the Sages of the Great Beit Din established at the beginning of the Second Temple period, headed by Ezra the Scribe, instituted that even when the majority of Israel is not in its Land, people would be obligated by rabbinic law to separate terumot, ma'asrot and ḥalla. They further instituted that even Jews living outside the Land would be obligated to separate ḥalla from their dough, so that the mitzva of ḥalla would not be forgotten by them. And why did they institute this for ḥalla and not for terumot and ma'asrot? Because the mitzva of ḥalla resembles to a certain extent the mitzvot that depend on the person and not on the land, since one becomes obligated in it at the time one kneads the dough (Tosafot, Kiddushin 36b; below 12:10). One can learn a profound idea from this enactment: in the merit of Israel's having fulfilled the mitzva of ḥalla in the Land of Israel throughout the days of the First Temple, the Sages were able to extend the obligation of the mitzva and the revelation of holiness to the dough that Israel makes outside the Land, and thereby connect all the creative activities that Jews perform outside the Land to the vision of the revelation of holiness that spreads from the Land to the entire world.

sections.title: The Mitzva of Ḥalla in Our Day
sections.html:
Following the destruction of the Second Temple and the dwindling of the Jewish community in the Land, the ability to become purified by means of the water of the ashes of the red heifer ceased, and consequently all kohanim are considered impure from contact with the dead, and it is forbidden for them to eat terumah and ḥalla (above 7:1). Nevertheless, the obligation of separating ḥalla remains in force, and the ḥalla is burned or buried in a place where people will not stumble by eating it. And as long as ḥalla has not been separated, the bread or cakes are forbidden to be eaten (the law outside the Land will be explained below, halakha 13). However, since in any case the ḥalla goes to waste, there is no need to separate one twenty-fourth of the dough as ḥalla; rather, it suffices to separate any amount whatsoever.

And although the mitzva today is rabbinic and the kohanim may not eat the ḥalla, through the mitzva of separating ḥalla we remember the vision, and our bread becomes connected to sacred values, and blessing is drawn into our homes. Therefore, some women have the custom to beautify the mitzva and bake an amount that obligates ḥalla on Erev Shabbat (Rema OḤ 242:1).

Regarding outside the Land: at the beginning of the Second Temple period, in accordance with the Sages' enactment, they would separate ḥalla outside the Land and eat it in purity. After several generations, the Sages decreed impurity upon the lands of the nations (below 12:9), and consequently the ḥalla separated outside the Land becomes impure and it is forbidden for kohanim to eat it. And so that people would not forget that ḥalla is intended to be eaten by the kohanim, the Sages instituted separating two ḥallot outside the Land: the first is burned, according to the law of impure ḥalla, which is forbidden to be eaten, and the second is eaten by the kohanim even when they are impure. Over time, in most communities of the Diaspora, the custom became accepted to separate only one ḥalla, and it is burned or buried. For the basis of the enactment of a second ḥalla outside the Land is to remember that ḥalla is intended to be eaten, as is practiced in the Land of Israel. And when in the Land of Israel the kohanim may not eat the ḥalla because of impurity, it is not fitting that outside the Land the kohanim should eat the ḥalla, and consequently outside the Land too one separates one ḥalla for burning (Rema OḤ 322:5 [?]; below 12:10).2

In summary: even today, when the kohanim may not eat the ḥalla, there is a rabbinic obligation upon every Jew, whether in the Land or outside the Land, to separate any amount whatsoever from the dough as ḥalla. When the majority of Israel lives in the Land, the obligation of the mitzva in the Land will once again be of Torah origin and blessing will increase, but it will still be forbidden for kohanim to eat the ḥalla because of impurity. When we merit the return of the order of purity to Israel, the kohanim will be able to reveal holiness in their lives and eat the ḥalla, and the blessing will grow stronger in Israel until it spreads openly to the entire world, and all the families of the earth will be blessed through us. And the allusion to the spreading of blessing to the entire world is in the enactment that the Sages instituted to separate ḥalla outside the Land as well.

sections.title: The Order of Separating Ḥalla in Practice
sections.html:
It is a mitzva to separate ḥalla from dough intended for baking whose flour is from the five species of grain (below halakha 8), and which contains a significant measure, from which food sufficient for at least an entire day can be prepared, that is, whose volume of flour is at least the volume of 43.2 eggs, about 2.160 liters (below halakha 6).

The mitzva applies to men and women alike, but if the husband and wife knead the dough together, she has precedence in the mitzva, because she is more responsible for household matters (see Or Zaru'a, end of 225; Rashi, Shabbat 32a).

One who separates ḥalla from the flour has not fulfilled the mitzva, for only after the flour and water are mixed does the obligation of the mitzva begin and it is possible to separate ḥalla, and the choicest time is at the completion of kneading the dough (SA 327:3).

Before fulfilling the mitzva one recites the blessing: "Blessed are You, Lord our God, King of the universe, who has sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us to separate ḥalla" (those of Yemenite descent and part of Ashkenaz), or "to separate ḥalla as terumah" (Eastern communities), or "to separate ḥalla from the dough" (many of Ashkenazic and North African descent).3

After the blessing, one separates a piece of any size, and some say at the time of separation: "Behold, this is ḥalla." Since it is forbidden to eat the ḥalla, it must be burned, so that people will not stumble by eating it. One may also place it in the garbage bin, and so that it will not be treated with disrespect, one should first wrap it and then place it in the garbage bin. And so many people do (above 9:5, note 8).4

If they forgot to separate ḥalla from the dough, they separate it after baking, and thereby permit the baked item. One who is concerned that perhaps ḥalla was not separated from a baked item that was served to him should separate a small crumb from it as ḥalla, and place it in a place where there is no concern that people will come to eat it.

From the time that girls and boys reach the age of mitzvot, they may fulfill the mitzva.5

A person may appoint a Jew as an agent to separate ḥalla from his dough on his behalf, and then the agent separates with a blessing. One may also appoint the cook as a permanent agent, to separate ḥalla from all the doughs he kneads throughout all the years of his work. But one who separates ḥalla contrary to the wishes of the owner of the dough – his separation is not effective (SA 328:3).

sections.title: The Measure That Obligates Ḥalla
sections.html:
The dough that is obligated in ḥalla is the dough that people used to prepare in the generation of the wilderness, as it is stated (Bamidbar 15:20): "Of the first of your dough (arisoteikhem) you shall set apart a cake (ḥalla) as a gift." "Arisa" is the dough that they would prepare from the manna that fell in the wilderness each day for each person, as it is stated (Shemot 16:16): "This is the thing that the Lord has commanded: Gather of it every man according to his eating, an omer a head, according to the number of your persons, shall you take it, every man for those who are in his tent." They would grind the manna and knead it into dough (Bamidbar 11:8), and its measure for each person was a tenth of an eifa, as it is stated (Shemot 16:36): "Now an omer is the tenth part of an eifa" (Eruvin 83b). But dough whose measure is less than this has no significance and is exempt from ḥalla.

A tenth of an eifa is a volume of forty-three and a fifth eggs – 2.160 liters (an egg being about 50 cc), and le-khatḥila it is good to round the calculation up to 2.200 liters. The calculation is of the flour before it is kneaded with water, and without additions of salt and spices. In order to be precise in the measure of the flour, one should measure it in vessels that have volume markings. When it is not possible to measure the volume, one makes use of calculating the measure by weight; however, since this is an estimate that depends on the degree of compression of the flour, there is doubt in it, for sometimes flour of the volume that obligates ḥalla weighs more and sometimes less. Therefore, it is necessary to establish two measures: one for the obligation to separate out of doubt without a blessing, and the second for the obligation to separate with a blessing. And since there are differences between types of flour, it is necessary to establish a measure for each flour, as explained in the table.6

Table (weights in kilograms):
Whole wheat – with a blessing (compressed flour): 1.650; without a blessing (loose flour): 1.450.
White wheat and spelt – with a blessing (compressed flour): 1.550; without a blessing (loose flour): 1.250.
Rye – with a blessing (compressed flour): 1.350; without a blessing (loose flour): 1.150.
Oats and barley – with a blessing (compressed flour): 1.200; without a blessing (loose flour): 1.050.

sections.title: Combining Doughs and Baked Goods
sections.html:
Doughs or baked goods, none of which individually contains the measure of ḥalla, that were combined together into the measure – one must separate ḥalla from them with a blessing. The combination is created in two ways: 1) When the two doughs stuck to each other during kneading or baking, such that if they were separated they would "bite" each other, that is, a little of the dough or baked item of one would be torn off onto the other. 2) When the doughs or baked goods are placed in one vessel or one bag, or when they are covered with a cloth – they combine to be considered one bread (SA 325:1). If the baked goods or doughs were placed in a refrigerator, a freezer, an oven, or a cabinet fixed in the wall, there is a doubt whether they combine – and therefore one should separate ḥalla from them without a blessing.7

One who does not wish to bake bread in the measure that obligates ḥalla need not bake more than his needs in order to fulfill the mitzva. But one who intends to bake the measure that obligates ḥalla may not divide it in two in order to exempt himself from the mitzva (Yerushalmi Ḥalla 3:1; SA 324:14). And even though the mitzva today is rabbinic, and the kohanim cannot eat the ḥalla because of impurity, it is forbidden to evade the mitzva, for through its fulfillment we connect to the idea hidden within it.

Two doughs or two baked items, each of which contains the measure of ḥalla – one may separate from one on behalf of the other as long as they are in one place, in the category of "mukaf" (as explained above 9:3). After the fact, if one separated not from the mukaf – he has fulfilled his obligation; and so the custom is le-khatḥila when people forgot to separate ḥalla and have already distributed the baked goods to other people, that one separates ḥalla from one baked item on behalf of baked goods that are in another place (SA 325:2; 331:25; above 9:3).

sections.title: Dough Intended to Be Divided Is Exempt
sections.html:
Two different doughs that one is particular not to mix, such as yeast dough and short-crust dough, do not combine. Moreover, even one dough that is going to be divided into two parts, half for a sweet baked item and half for a savory baked item – even though it is now one dough, the parts that are going to be divided do not combine (SA 326:1).

Women who kneaded dough together so that each of them would take her portion for herself – even though the shared dough contains the measure of ḥalla, since they are going to divide it, it does not combine into the measure. And even if they bake everything in one oven, as long as each one recognizes her baked item and is particular to take it for herself, the baked goods do not combine into the measure.

Therefore, women who wish to bake breads or cakes together in order to merit the mitzva, if none of them has the measure of ḥalla on her own, must be careful to be full partners in all the baked goods until the completion of baking, and after the baking each one should take her portion for herself at random, that is, without there being a marking that this is her baked item; in this way one of them can separate ḥalla on behalf of all of them. But if each one braids dough for herself in a special form and is particular to take it afterward, since they divided the doughs before baking, their doughs do not combine. Likewise, a kindergarten teacher who bakes ḥallot with the children in preparation for Shabbat, where each child kneads his own dough and his name is stuck on it – their ḥallot do not combine.8

sections.title: The Flour and the Liquids
sections.html:
The mitzva is to separate ḥalla from dough intended for baking bread, as it is stated (Bamidbar 15:19): "then it shall be that when you eat of the bread of the land." Therefore, the dough obligated in the mitzva is dough made from one of the five species of grain, which are: wheat, barley, spelt, oats and rye. Their uniqueness is that they can become leavened, and therefore one can make bread and cakes from their dough, and when one is careful that they not become leavened, one can make matzot for the mitzva on Pesaḥ from them. But one who makes a baked item from corn flour or rice flour is not obligated in ḥalla, since their dough cannot become leavened and is not called bread, and therefore it is also impossible to make matzot for Pesaḥ from them (Peninei Halakha: Pesaḥ 2:3). It is worth noting that there is a species of legume called kusemet (buckwheat), and even if flour is made from it, it is not obligated in ḥalla, since it is not a species of grain.

One who mixed flours of the five species of grain and made from them one dough containing the measure of ḥalla – it is obligated in ḥalla (SA 324:2). One who mixed flours of the five species of grain with other ingredients, such as cornflour, sugar, cocoa and eggs – if three conditions are met in the mixture, one separates ḥalla with a blessing:
1) the baked item has the taste of grain; 2) the flour of the species of grain contains the measure of ḥalla;
3) the species of grain are the majority – one separates ḥalla with a blessing. And if the third condition is not met, that is, the baked item has the taste of grain and the measure of ḥalla, but the species of grain are not the majority – one separates ḥalla without a blessing. And if one of the first two conditions is not met, that is, the baked item does not have the taste of grain, or the grain does not contain the measure of ḥalla – it is exempt from ḥalla.9

One who kneads the flour with significant liquids is obligated in ḥalla. Six of the seven significant liquids are permitted for eating, and they are: water, dew, olive oil, wine, milk and bees' honey (the seventh, blood, is forbidden to be eaten). But if one kneaded the flour with other liquids, such as fruit juice or egg liquid, there is a doubt whether the dough is obligated in ḥalla, and one should separate ḥalla without a blessing. However, if a little water is added to the fruit juice, one must separate ḥalla with a blessing.10

sections.title: Dough for Baking – Bread
sections.html:
As we have learned, the mitzva is to separate ḥalla from dough intended for baking bread, as it is stated (Bamidbar 15:19-21): "then it shall be that when you eat of the bread of the land … of the first of your dough (your dough) you shall give to the Lord a gift throughout your generations." Included in "bread" are all grain baked goods, such as cakes, crackers, biscuits, baked goods filled with meat, cheese or vegetables, bagels, pretzel sticks and baklava. However, over bread people customarily establish a meal, and therefore over it one always recites "Ha-motzi" and Birkat Ha-mazon, whereas the other baked goods are intended for casual eating, and therefore only when one establishes a meal over them does one recite "Ha-motzi" and Birkat Ha-mazon, and when one eats them in their usual manner, casually, one recites over them "Mezonot" and "Al Ha-miḥya." By contrast, over cooked grain dishes, such as ptitim (toasted pasta pellets) and noodles, even if one establishes a meal, one always recites "Mezonot" and "Al Ha-miḥya," for since they are a cooked dish and not a baked item, they are not bread. This is the rule: a grain baked item is called bread, and it is a mitzva to separate ḥalla from it; and a cooked grain dish is not bread, and there is no mitzva to separate ḥalla from it (this is the opinion of most poskim, as explained in the next halakha).

Cooking and baking are both done with heat, but cooking is done within boiling liquids, whereas a baked item, although it contains liquids, thanks to which it is baked and not burned, is not placed within liquids while it is being baked. Generally baking is done in an oven, but one can also prepare baked goods in a frying pan or a pot placed on a fire. And even though people customarily put a little oil on their bottom so that the dough will not stick, or in order to add flavor to it, since the liquids around the dough are minimal, they are considered baked goods. Therefore, one must separate ḥalla with a blessing from baked goods such as malawaḥ and mufleta, which are baked in a frying pan, and kubaneh and jaḥnun, which are baked in a pot; and if one establishes a meal over them, one recites "Ha-motzi" and Birkat Ha-mazon.11

sections.title: Thick Dough Intended for Cooking
sections.html:
When one intends to make from the dough sufganiyot (doughnuts), noodles, ptitim, dumplings (kreplach) or soup croutons (shkedei marak) – since one intends to prepare them for eating by cooking in water or frying in deep oil, they are exempt from ḥalla. And some say that all these doughs are obligated in ḥalla, because the time of the obligation of ḥalla is at the kneading of the dough, and since their dough is thick and fit for baking as bread, even though the intention is to cook them, one must separate ḥalla from them (Rabbeinu Tam). In practice, the halakha follows the opinion of most poskim, that since one intends to cook these doughs, they are not considered bread, and even if one establishes a meal over them, their blessing is "Mezonot" and "Al Ha-miḥya." However, le-khatḥila, in order to satisfy all opinions, the custom is to separate ḥalla from them without a blessing.12

If one bakes part of the dough that one intends to cook, even the size of a small cookie, according to all opinions one will be obligated to separate ḥalla with a blessing from that baked item. And this is the advice for one who wishes to resolve the doubt and merit the mitzva: to decide in advance to bake a small cookie from the dough in the oven or in a frying pan (Maharam of Rothenburg; SA 329:4).13

sections.title: Liquid Batter – Blintzes and Laḥoḥ
sections.html:
As a rule, dough intended for baking is a thick dough, and by contrast, when one prepares a liquid batter for cooking, such as porridge and soups containing a lot of flour, they are exempt from ḥalla, and even if one eats from them the measure of a full meal, one recites "Mezonot" and "Al Ha-miḥya."

However, sometimes the liquid batter is poured into a pot, a baking pan or a frying pan, and there it gradually becomes a baked item, such as ḥavitiyot (small pancakes). And since they have the form of bread, that is, the form of a baked item – one must separate ḥalla from them, and if one establishes a meal over them, one recites over them "Ha-motzi" and Birkat Ha-mazon. However, the obligation to separate ḥalla takes effect upon them only at the completion of their baking, for while they are batter they are not considered bread dough (Ha-teruma; Torat Ha-aretz vol. 1, 4:92-93). And one should note that even after baking they become obligated in ḥalla only if their flour contains the measure of obligation; and since usually a single baked item does not contain the measure obligating ḥalla, only if several baked items are combined together (as explained above in halakha 7) must one separate ḥalla from them.

The same is the law of pancakes, laḥoḥ, blintzes, Belgian waffles and the like: since they have the form of bread, that is, the form of a baked item – meaning that they have a thickness created by the rising of baking – they are obligated in ḥalla, and if one eats from them the measure of a full meal, one recites "Ha-motzi" and Birkat Ha-mazon. But if they were made especially thin, they do not have the form of a baked item and are exempt from ḥalla, and even if one eats from them the measure of a full meal, one recites "Mezonot" and "Al Ha-miḥya." When there is a doubt whether they are regular or especially thin, one separates ḥalla without a blessing.14

sections.title: Various Laws
sections.html:
Ḥalla that became mixed into the dough: If ḥalla was separated and then became mixed back into the dough, if the dough was a hundred times its amount, the ḥalla is nullified. If the dough was not a hundred times its amount, the dough is forbidden. And if they have not yet begun eating from the baked item, the one who separated the ḥalla can go to a Sage, who sits together with two other people as a beit din, and they annul for him the separation of the ḥalla retroactively. For the separation of ḥalla is like a vow, and just as one can annul a vow, so one can annul the separation of ḥalla (Rema 323:1). The one requesting annulment should say before them that he regrets having separated ḥalla, and had he known that it would become mixed into the dough he would not have separated it. And they say to him three times: "It is permitted to you" or "The ḥalla is annulled," and thereby the dough or baked item becomes permitted, and he must separate ḥalla from it again without a blessing (Halakhot Ketanot 1:48; Birkei Yosef 323:2; Yabi'a Omer YD 1:21; and according to the Ḥatam Sofer YD 320, one should recite the blessing. The same law applies to terumot and ma'asrot, above 9:4, note 7).

Ḥalla outside the Land: As we have learned (in halakhot 3-4), the Sages instituted separating ḥalla outside the Land as well, and even though at a time when the majority of Israel is not in the Land, the mitzva of ḥalla is rabbinic in the Land too, the mitzva of separation outside the Land is more lenient, since it is fundamentally rabbinic. The central expression of this is that in the Land of Israel one must separate ḥalla from the mukaf, that is, if one wishes to separate from one dough on behalf of another dough, when each of them contains the measure of ḥalla, both must be in the same place (as explained in halakha 7); but outside the Land one may separate even on behalf of dough that is not in the same place. Not only that, but it is permitted to bake the dough and begin eating from it, and only toward the end of eating it to separate ḥalla from it on behalf of what has already been eaten (SA 323:1).

Shabbat: Just as it is forbidden to separate terumot and ma'asrot on Shabbat, so it is forbidden to separate ḥalla on Shabbat (SA OḤ 339:4; MB 26; above 10:4). One who is concerned that he will not manage to separate ḥalla before Shabbat begins can make a stipulation and say: "What I will separate on Shabbat as ḥalla, behold it is ḥalla," and on Shabbat he recites the blessing and separates ḥalla, as explained above (10:4, note 1). Outside the Land, as we have learned, it is permitted to eat from the baked item and leave a little for after Shabbat, and separate ḥalla from it (Rema OḤ 506:3; MB 21).

Ḥalla of a gentile: The dough of a gentile is exempt from the mitzva of ḥalla, and even if a Jew kneads the dough for him, the dough is exempt. Therefore, a bakery owned by gentiles, even if all the workers are Jews, is exempt from separating ḥalla. And unlike terumot, where if the gentile wishes to separate terumah his terumah becomes sanctified, with ḥalla, even if he separates, his ḥalla does not become sanctified (SA and Rema 330:1; 331:44; above 8:11). And one tells this to the gentile, so that he will know that there is no need to be particular that specifically kohanim eat the ḥalla he separated (Shakh 330:3). Dough in which a Jew and a gentile are partners – if the Jew's portion contains flour in the measure obligating ḥalla, the Jew's portion is obligated in ḥalla (SA 330:3).
